Surely you do not think we are fools enough, now that we have passed them, to go back upon them? Surely you are not going to ask us to reverse what we did?" We have a right to ask the government to do so, for the reason that before it took the step we challenged its soundness as applied to Canada; we challenged the virtue of its course; we declared these results would follow. Therefore we are in a position to call upon the government to remedy injuries done by itself.
The French treaty can be passed over very quickly; it has been before parliament and under debate many times. A very few comments on its consequences will illustrate its value. In the French treaty there did not appear from the beginning one single concession offered this country save in respect of a few spare parts of farm implements, which obtained entry into France on a little better terms. In every other regard, wherever this treaty touched the actual exports of Canada, the government brought to this House a treaty which raised the duties against them, or which did not affect them at all. In not one single other particular did the government come to parliament with duties against the actual exports of this country lower than before. On the contrary, in relation to some of our most valuable exports the government brought back a treaty under which the duty against our
products entering France was fifty per cent higher than before the treaty was entered into at all. The government told us the treaty was the best it could do. We criticized the government at the time, on the ground that before it ventured to enter into a treaty with France-which had raised its tariff anywhere from four to twelve times over, it was bound in justice to this country to raise the Canadian duties on products in respect of which France would want concessions from us. The government ridiculed our suggestion; it intimated that it was against its policy. With arms tied behind their back, by their own folly, members of the government went over to negotiate a treaty with France. Now I ask any member of the administration to tell me one article in the whole range of Canadian exports which he can show fiom the trade returns was benefited by that treaty.
The Minister of Railways-either the Minister of Railways or the ex-Minister-told the people down in South Essex that the farmers had done better with their hogs because of the treaties the government had made. But not in respect of hogs, or anything else, has the government opened a market; it has not opened a market for the single product of a Canadian farm.	In
respect of products of major consequence, the government virtually killed the industry so far as exports to France are concerned. The member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) showed from the returns of the Trade and Commerce department that where we sold four and a half million pounds of condensed milk before the treaty was entered into, we sold France last year only eighty thousand pounds of that article, and the year before less than a million pounds. Why? The treaty raised the duty on condensed milk by fifty per cent and killed the trade with France. The treaty raised the duty on canned salmon fifty per cent and seriously damaged that trade; and we stand to-day with a balance of trade against us of seven millions where we had seven millions in our favour before hon. gentlemen opposite ventured on the negotiation.
In respect of Italy we are buying now from that country a few hundred thousand dollars more than we were when the treaty was entered into, and we are selling to Italy $8,000,000 less than before hon. gentlemen put their blundering hands on our trade with that country.

If you can win over the horticulturist, the truck farmer, you will have a good point of vantage as regards the dairyman and some day as regards the cattle man and maybe the wheat man. My hon. friends believe in climbing up a step at a time and I do not blame them for that. Frankly speaking, I am one of those who believe and have believed for some time that their tactics are going to get a measure of success, because the appeal to self interest is the most powerful appeal when you come to political questions. If you can persuade any class of farmers that protection will pay, you will win over those farmers because farmers are no better than any other Canadians.
Does the hon. member imply that the five Progressives who voted contrary to his party are more selfish than the rest of the Progressives?

Not at all. I have known
three of them a good deal longer than I have known the hon. gentleman and I am sufficiently well acquainted with them to know that they stand high in the esteem of the Progressive party. I am sure that any course they have taken this session is as conscientious as any course I have followed myself. When discussing this matter just now I was merely pointing out that the temptation to vote against the government was very real to all Progressives, including these five gentlemen and no one outside of the Progressive party will know how real it was.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen to my right
should accustom themselves to have the very best opinions of the motives of others. The Canadian farmer is no different from the American farmer, and if the American farmer has chosen protection I see nothing to prevent the Canadian farmer from doing the same if he believes that he can derive any benefit

from so doing. But the going for our protectionist friends will become heavier and heavier as they get away from the truck farmers to the grain growers.	The ease
with which they have converted the small farmers on the fringe of the big cities is no index to the job they will have on their hands if they attempt to convert the grain growers of this country. I regret to say it, but I think that this is a right estimate of the average Canadian farmer. They are not all like my hon. friend to my left (Mr. Evans), who would advocate theoretical free trade through thick and thin. There is a big sprinkling of such free traders through the west, but I do not think that the average Canadian farmer is just like that; and if our friends want to make a breach in the geoera-tion^old phalanx of rural Canada they must do a lot of persuading, and they must not be too particular on what they base tiheir persuasion. They must appeal to self interest.
The American farmers have accepted protection, but there is one thing that hon. gentlemen have forgotten, and that is that the American farmers, having experienced protection for two or three years, are at the present time agitating for the privilege of fixing prices on wheat. Now I want to say something that has not been frequently said in this House; it has not been said for the reason that the position of the farmers' organizations of this country has not been apprehended by members of this House. Since the beginning of last parliament we have seen grow up in western Canada one of the biggest co-operative organizations in the world, which to-day is marketing 70 or 80 per cent of its wheat through one channel. What does that mean? It means that in a short time the farmers of the wesit will all be marketing their product through the same channel. And what are these Canadian farmers going to do? If we take hon. gentlemen at their word, and believe with them that Canada has for all time decided for protection, what is the commonsense wheat grower of the west going to do?
Are you speaking for the wheat farmer or the man who is engaged in diversified farming?

The question is a polite one but I do not see its relevancy. I was talking about the wheat pool and I was saying that if what our friends contend is true, that Canada has for all time to come accepted protection as the policy for this country, then something must happen within the ranks of the organized farmers of Canada. If you can persuade the farmers of this country that

The Address-Mr. Bird
protection has come to stay, then they are going to come to parliament and, if the Conservatives happen to be in power, they will say, "Now then, your brick for brick policy fits in very nicely. We want 40 per cent of a duty on wheat and if the United States duty goes up to 70 cents, then brick by tbrick the Canadian farmer will demand that the tariff on this side be built up to that level". Then, poetic justice coming to pass, what will happen with a body of farmers controlling a stable commodity marketed through then-own agency? They are going to fix prices just as much as the Ford motor works fix their prices. That will be the outcome, and when that happens the theory of protection will explode in universal derision. The part of the body politic who are at present unprovided for will at last have got their feet into the trough and will shove the other hogs along and out in order that they may share in the contents. You say that this is a very imaginary picture I am drawing, but it is not; it is very present in the minds of the farmers to the south of us in the Dakotas and in the wheat growing areas generally in the United States. And more than that, it has got to be practical politics there. It is very well known that the late Secretary of Agriculture in the United States, in the postwar period, was in favour of a price fixing arrangement whereby the American farmer could sell his product on the home market at a price that would recoup him for the cost of production. Let me quote from Henry C. Wallace's book, Our Debt and Duty to the Farmer. At page 200 he says:
The sole purpose of the McNary-Haugen Bill was to re-establish and maintain the normal pre-war ratio between the prices of agricultural crops of which we produce an exportable surplus and the general commodity-price index, thus putting agriculture somewhat near an equality with industry and labour.
Then again at page 202:
This bill met with astonishingly violent opposition. It was fought by grain dealers and exporters who thought it might interfere with their business; by laissez-faire economists; by those who want nothing done to relieve discontent which makes grist for their political mill; by opponents of the protective tariff system who saw in this an application to farm needs of the tariff principle; by representatives of the industrial interests who want nothing done to increase domestic prices of food products; and by many who did not study the measure for themselves but accepted at par the unintelligent criticisms made against it.
Now that is proof beyond all doubt that a
movement is on the way in protectionist America whereby the farmers may recoup themselves for the cost of their production- and in the United States they have no wheat pool.
14011-69J
May I ask the hon. gentleman, if the Australian treaty protects the Australian farmers on eggs to the extent of 18 cents a dozen, what objection has he to that so far as our farmers are concerned?

I am dealing at present with
the price-fixing problem that' will be precipitated if my hon. friends get their way. In Canada the wheat farmers are in an infinitely better position to take advantage of this kind of thing than the United States farmers have ever been; and as I say, if it is true that protection has come for good, then for these men on the western plains who have to send their surplus to Europe it seems to me there is only one issue: they should use their combined selling effort in order to do exactly what the manufacturers want to do under protection-raise the price of wheat to a point where it will pay them for their labour and invested capital. I do not think they will ever want 10 per cent like the Canadian Pacific Railway, or 20 per cent like the banks; but they surely have the right to demand that their return on their product should be equivalent to what they have invested in the way of labour and capital.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my voice is getting weak. My purpose in rising was not to go into these matters very extensively, but to give the House an opportunity to say whether it had had enough of amendments or not. Therefore I beg to move the following motion, seconded by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans):
That this question be now put.

Is it the pleasure of the
House to adopt the motion?

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that
moving the previous question permits one to discuss the whole matter at length. Therefore, unless the leader of the House desires me to continue, I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
